title: You Should, You Could, You Must -- The Rule and the Exception
desc: Modals for obligation, advice and deduction, in the call where the client wants an exception. Key expressions: policy, compliance, waiver, refund, to escalate, guidelines, fare, to comply with, grace period, penalty, to flag, approval chain. Structure: must, have to, should, could and might -- and why must not and do not have to are opposites.
vocab: Policy
an official rule that a company follows
Company policy says we must charge the fee, and I cannot change that.
Compliance
following the rules and laws that apply to your work
Compliance has to approve any discount over that limit.
Waiver
an official document that lets one case not follow a normal rule
I can request a waiver, but I cannot promise it will be approved.
Refund
money given back to a customer
A full refund is not possible, but the ticket could stay open for a year.
To escalate
to pass a problem to somebody more senior
I cannot approve it, but I can escalate it today.
Guidelines
advice about how something should be done, not a strict rule
The guidelines say ten days, but you can depart from them with a reason.
Fare
the price a passenger pays for a flight
The fare rules are in the contract, and they apply to every ticket.
To comply with
to do what a rule or a law requires
Every corporate contract has to comply with the same fare rules.
Grace period
extra time you are allowed after a deadline before a penalty applies
There is a twenty-four hour grace period, and you are still inside it.
Penalty
an amount you pay or a consequence when a rule is broken
After that date the penalty is higher than the ticket.
To flag
to mark something so that other people notice it needs attention
I will flag the invoice so that finance looks at it today.
Approval chain
the sequence of people who must approve something
The approval chain has three names on it, and mine is not one of them.

paras: A client calls on a Monday morning with twelve tickets on the wrong day. He knows what the answer is going to be, and he calls anyway, which is a good sign: he would rather learn the rule than argue with it.

There are three levels, and mixing them up is what makes these calls go badly. Level one is the policy. If the contract says the change fee applies, it applies, and nobody can remove it by being sympathetic. Every corporate contract has to comply with the same fare rules. Level two is the guidelines: recommendations you should follow, and may depart from if you can explain why. Level three is the exception, which must be requested, must have a reason attached, and must be approved by somebody in the approval chain.

So Rosa does three things on the call. She states the rule first, because a client who hears the rule early stops hoping. Then she offers what she could do instead: no refund, but the tickets stay open for twelve months. Then she is honest about the limit — she can request a waiver and she can escalate it today, but she must not promise it before compliance approves it.

The last thirty seconds are the ones that keep the client. He asks what he should do differently, and she gives him exactly one thing: call before booking more than six seats, because there is a grace period on the group fare that almost nobody knows about, and after it the penalty is higher than the ticket. Then she says she will flag the invoice so that finance looks at it the same day.
quiz: Why does the text say "we must charge the fee" and not "we should charge the fee"?
Because it is advice, and he can ignore it.
Because it is a rule in the contract, with no choice involved.
Because it is a guess about the invoice.
What is the difference between guidelines and policy, according to the text?
Guidelines are recommendations you may depart from with a reason; policy is a rule.
They are two words for the same thing.
"She must not promise it before it is approved." What does that mean?
It is optional, and she can decide.
It is forbidden until the approval comes.
She is not required to, but it would help.
Why does she tell him about the grace period?
Because it is the answer to what he should do differently next time.
Because it removes the fee on this booking.

tip.title: Modals -- Obligation, Advice, Options and Guesses
tip.intro: Five small words, and each one sets a different temperature. You already know all of them. What this lesson trains is choosing the right one without stopping to think.
rows: Obligation, no choice. Must often comes from the rule itself, have to from an outside circumstance. In most business sentences they are interchangeable.

"We must charge the fee."
"Compliance has to approve it."
Advice and recommendation. Strong enough to be useful, soft enough not to offend.
An option, or a possibility you are not sure about. The polite way to put an idea on the table.

"We could keep the ticket open."
"It might be the fare class."
Must also means I am almost certain, when you are reading evidence instead of stating a rule.
"That must be the old fare — the contract changed in March."
must not = forbidden. do not have to = optional. They are opposites, and confusing them changes the whole message.

"You must not promise it." (forbidden)
"You do not have to copy me." (optional)
tip.note: After every modal comes the base verb: no to, no -s, no -ing. She must call, never she must to call and never she musts call.

must
Hint: it is a rule and there is no choice
Under the contract we must charge the change fee.
charge the change fee.

Hint: this is advice, not an obligation
You should call me before you book more than six seats.
call me before you book more than six seats.
We

Hint: an option you are offering, not a promise
We could leave the tickets open for twelve months.
leave the tickets open for twelve months.

Hint: a guess you are not sure about

be the fare class, but I am not sure.

Hint: it is forbidden -- not merely optional
I must not promise the exception before it is approved.

Hint: this one is optional, and that is the opposite of forbidden
You do not have to copy the regional office on every email.

order.intro: Listen to the summary of the call with the corporate client, then put the steps in the correct order.
items: Gustavo explains that the meeting moved and that twelve tickets now have to be changed.
Rosa says that the change fee applies under the contract and that she cannot remove it.
Gustavo asks whether there is anything at all that can be done.
Rosa offers to escalate a waiver request and explains what has to go with it.
Gustavo asks what he should do differently next time, and Rosa gives him one concrete rule.

speech: Under the contract we must charge the change fee.
What we could do instead is leave the tickets open for a year.
I must not promise it before it is approved.
I cannot approve it, but I can escalate it today.
You should call me before you book more than six seats.

quiz.intro: A client wants an exception and a new colleague wants to know the rules. Choose the best thing to say.
items: The client asks you to remove a fee the contract applies. Your first sentence is:
No, that is impossible.
Under the contract we must charge the fee, and here is what we could do instead.
We must to charge the fee, sorry.
You want to advise him about next time. You say:
You should call me before you book more than six seats.
You shoulds call me before you book more than six seats.
You must to call me before you book more than six seats.
A colleague asks whether he needs to copy the regional office on every email. He does not. You say:
You must not copy the regional office on every email.
You do not have to copy the regional office on every email.
You cannot copy the regional office on every email.
You want to tell him that promising an unapproved exception is forbidden. You say:
You do not have to promise the exception before it is approved.
You must not promise the exception before it is approved.
You should not to promise the exception before it is approved.
The invoice shows a price you do not recognize. You are almost sure why. You say:
That should be the old fare.
That must be the old fare -- the contract changed in March.
That must to be the old fare.

think: Think of one real request from a client that you had to refuse, and record about ninety seconds handling it in English. Say the rule first with must or have to, offer one alternative with could, be honest about the limit with must not or cannot, and finish with one piece of advice using should. Do not start any sentence with the word no.
survival: Under the contract we must charge the change fee.
What we could do instead is leave the tickets open for a year.
I must not promise it before it is approved.
I cannot approve it, but I can escalate it today.
You should call me before you book more than six seats.
